text:
32:29 750W Power Supply or not. Efficiency matters a LOT actually. I don't understand why people can't see that efficiency is LITERALLY EXTRA COST you have to pay.

If a card has slightly less performance but significantly better efficiency,  over the time of ownership that could save you quite a lot of money.
Let's say your card uses 100W more power and you game 3 hours per day on average for 3 years. That's 100W * 3h * 365 * 3 = 328.5 kWh
Let's say you pay 0.2$ per kWh. That's 328.5 kWh *  0.2$/kWh = 65.7$

That's a significant part of the way towards the next performance tier part. 
Same goes for CPUs btw. That's the reason I still went for Zen3 despite the price hike over intel. Over the probably 5 years I'm probably gonna use it, it's saving me way more than what I'd save in upfront price buying intel right now. 
But of course you have to see how your usage profile is likely to be to make a good estimation.


tl;dr
Lower power consumption = significant amount of money saved 
-> Could be used to buy higher tier but more efficient alternative from the other team. Do the easy calculation and profit!

text: A small comment about VRAM usage for Doom Eternal versus the RTX 2080.  The stock RTX 2080 has VRAM bandwidth of 448 GB/sec.  At 88 FPS, this grants the average frame memory bandwidth of 5.09 GB/frame, which is less than the 8GB VRAM capacity.  Using the 71 fps figure for the worst case scenario, each frame had 6.3 GB of memory bandwidth.  Extra comparison of frame rate versus bandwidth at the lowered texture setting, that 111fps shares equivalent bandwidth usage with the RTX 3080's 189 fps.  This really points out that Doom Eternal spent additional memory bandwidth juggling used objects in VRAM, not efficiently prioritizing which objects are loaded in VRAM at a time.  Given this bandwidth includes both read and write, that 6.3GB per frame bandwidth suggests that much less than 6 GB of VRAM was actively used per frame in the Ultra Nightmare settings.  The amount of data needed to be read can easily fit in the 8GB VRAM, but the engine just needed to manage the data in VRAM better.

text: I think Gamers Nexus did these tests and graphs better, using their latest testing methods, and acknowledging that Ryzen CPU's make very poor partners in a GPU testing system. A small gain you mention offhand is still a gain, it's still a sign you muddy the waters using the CPU you guys did for the shown tests. PCIE 3.0 didn't bottleneck the 2080ti, and it doesn't bottleneck the 3080 by much, if at all. Especially compared to using a CPU with too many cores for most games to bother with and too low a frequency to sate their demands. I'm sorry but for a clearer comparison for gaming focused applications, people should look at GN. As they already proved, what CPU you use does matter. It already mattered clearly with the 2080ti. A gamer seeking to get the most out of their high end GPU will not use AMD CPUs if they are smart. Unless they finally give us the frequency boost needed with Zen 3.
If you're here to argue over a 2% difference overall at 1440p, well then I really don't have time for that nonsense. Not to mention a 0% difference at 4K, it's just ridiculous really.

text:
The 3080 almost needs to be compared to an overclocked 2080ti pulling 320W. The reason being that 320W is an entirely new class of card irrespective of the naming scheme or price.

Using Steves numbers at 1440p average of just 21% faster, that's lower than the 25% additional power draw.
With 4K only managing 31% average over the 2080ti, while that's ahead of the 25% additional power draw it ends up in single digit territory.

Is Nvidia having a Vega moment and is their architecture unable to scale without throwing a lot more power at it.

The 3090 with only 20% more cores should only improve on the 2080 by 10% with exception to memory limited scenarios, meaning where's the space for the 3080ti except for more memory and 5% performance gains with exception to memory limited scenarios to the 3080, which means no 20GB 3080 as that would make both the 3080ti and 3090 pointless cards except for maybe productivity and even then. I suspect that the rumoured 3080ti is the 20 GB "3080" or there will be no 3080ti.

I can see a Titan X Pascal vs 1080ti vs Titan Xp scenario happening all over again with the 3090, when they made the 1080ti as powerful (minus 1GB memory) as the Titan X Pascal and then made the Titan Xp.

The 3090 will just get you extra VRAM and performance now and that's what you will be paying the premium for. Expect it to be obsolete by the 2nd quarter 2021.

Honestly if Big Navi lives up to expectations of 80CU (5120SP) and 50% efficiency gains with scalability (that's the key element), then Ampere might only be saved by raytracing and Nvidia specific productivity (e.g. NVENC) applications, because the 3080 just isn't fast enough for the maths of RDNA claims and borderline if scalability turns to crap after 40CU's (like Vega did).

text:
If you are going to investigate VRAM dependent performance, because so many people are scared that 10GB won't be enough, please also include some real world gaming scenarios, like using Nvidias shadowplay. Afterburner also supports GPU encoding and "pre-recording" which can be buffered to either your drive or directly in the VRAM. You can limit the buffer to either time, or size. This could theoretically also be used to artificially inflate VRAM usage to see when performance drops occur. If you use CPU encoding instead, it will be buffered into the system RAM. Would be really interesting to see when RAM usage affects performance and in which scenarios you will be bottlenecked by the different encoding options. At low resolutions, CPU encoding would probably be a bottleneck, while it would be the GPU at high resolutions. Also how many threads can you use for encoding without a performance loss (perfect multi tasking test for Ryzen CPUs from 6 to 16 cores)

The RTX voice beta showed a gaming performance decrease, when it was in use. It would be nice to know how these features for gamers, like Nvidia Broadcast affect performance.

text:
24:00 I have to admit that I'm quite surprised that there wasn't a larger difference between PCIe 3.0 and 4.0 considering the results from the 5700XT. In F1 2020, the 5700XT was about 2% faster in avg performance across all 3 resolutions, while 1% low performance increased by 5% at 1080p, 3% at 1440p, and 1% at 4K when moving from PCIe 3.0 x16 to PCIe 4.0 x16. But the 3080 sees a smaller difference. The best is 3% higher avg performance at 1080p, but this drops to 2% at 1440p and 0% at 4K, while 1% low sees just a 1% increase across all 3 resolutions.

I had expected the difference from PCIe 3.0 to PCIe 4.0 to grow larger with a faster graphics card, not get slower. Especially not when the 3080 is between 50 and 90% faster than the 5700XT in F1 2020 (50% faster avg at 1440p, 90% faster 1% low at 4K). 
What's going on here? Why is the difference lower with the 3080 than the 5700XT?

I look forward to more tests on PCIe 4.0. Especially with Death Stranding and Horizon Zero Dawn as these are the newer titles. PCIe 4.0 gave the 5700XT 3-6% higher frame rates in Death Stranding, and that includes 4K results. Will the 3080 be able to take advantage of PCIe 4.0 in that title?

I can't wait for the upcoming tests! Today marked the start of the most exciting couple of months for hardware enthusiasts we've seen in several years with both Ampere, RDNA2, and Zen 3 set up to deliver huge jumps across the board. And your amazing benchmarks just makes it so much better :D

text:
I hope you'll also be exploring scaling on a PCIe x8 link at some point.

I think usage of the secondary PCIe slot for NVMe storage will become more and more common:

- Once more high-performance PCIe 4 drives using new controllers enter the market, and software becomes capable of taking advantage of their speed (e.g. DirectStorage), people will want to add one to their system in addition to their old PCIe 3 drive.

- Some motherboards only have a single dedicated M.2 slot.

- On existing Intel platforms, the possible multiple M.2 slots often share bandwidth thru a single chipset connection equivalent to PCIe 3 x4 - not only with each other, but most other peripherals and SATA storage.

author: @Koozwad

text:
@Koozwad  This is a bit misguided as all the reviewers have pointed out so far - the 3080 does not in any way have too little VRAM for 4k. It's simply not the case. I would not worry about gaming at more than 4k for the next 10 years, so no real need to worry about futureproofing... The GPU will be so outdated at that point it'll be useless anyhow.

Something like >97% of Steam users still play at lower than 4k resolution. You're already in an extreme minority in that sense. And besides, if you're gaming at 4k, you're playing at 60FPS - unless you have a 4000$ monitor, putting you in the like 0.0001% of users. VRAM is not an issue if your target is 4k60. Probably not an issue even if you're targeting 4k120.
author: @Mythricia1988

text: @Mythricia1988  Some games even now(such as Doom Eternal) can hit at least 9GB VRAM already without any mods. Just imagine in the next few years... When you buy a card, especially one as expensive as a 3080 you expect to get at least a few years out of it. It's important to be futureproofed at least a few years. Most people don't upgrade every 2 years.
author: @Koozwad

text:
@Koozwad  Gamers Nexus specifically pointed out how this assumption is wrong - a GPU monitoring app saying the VRAM usage is 90% or whatever, does not actually mean the game is requiring 90% of the VRAM. It means it has ALLOCATED that much VRAM, this is different from usage. Another example of this is CoD Warzone that always allocates basically 100% of VRAM, no matter what GPU you use - but with no performance difference at all. That is because it has requested the memory but is not actually using all of it. All games do this to some degree CoDWZ is just an extreme example. Doom Eternal is no different.

author: @Mythricia1988

text:
@Koozwad  This thread literally confirms what I TOLD YOU. Excerpt:

==================
There are effects buffers, shadow buffers, stencil buffers, z buffers, ping-pong buffers, etc. For a breakdown of ram required for a deferred renderer, bare-minimum, see this post:

http://techreport.com/forums/viewtopic.php?f=3&t=90126#p1182424

Also, don't forget that for 3D, we use 64 bits per-pixel for most shader operations, not 32 bits like in 2D.

TLDR: (and these numbers change depending on the game):

1920x1080 4xMSAA = 187.113MiB

2560x1440 4xMSAA = 316.313MiB

3840x2160 4xMSAA = 685.453MiB

The sizes still scale linearly with resolution, there's just several more buffers than people expect, and they are larger than people expect. Still, assets use the majority of vram.
================

So like I said, almost no difference going based on resolution alone. Definitely nothing about the increased buffer sizes going from 1080 to 4K is going to magically eat up 4GB++ of VRAM. It's bullshit, stop spreading it. What uses more VRAM are larger assets. Assets don't grow because you render at a higher resolution. Assets grow because you picked a higher texture resolution option / higher graphics setting. This is independent and irrelevant to 4K, 2K, 1080p, whatever.

text: @shredderorokusaki3013  Dude that 60Hz monitor and R7 1700 CPU are serious bottlenecks for an RTX3080. You'll be better off with an RTX3070 and R5 3600 (which should work with your current motherboard). Your framerates will still go higher than 60Hz but maybe you could overclock the monitor to 75Hz. I recently upgraded my 1600X (all core overclocked to 4.05GHz) with a 3900XT (currently stock) and noticed quite a big difference in many games (in 1440p) and that's only with a 1080Ti. And as we've just seen the 3080 is much more powerful than my 1080Ti and a 1700 clocks lower than a 1600X. So buying a 3080 without upgrading the CPU and/or the monitor for a 4K one is a waste. Especially because the RYZEN 3000 models are becoming increasingly cheaper. An R5 3600 starts at €184 where I live, a 3700X starts at €290. Both work with your old motherboard (with a BIOS update), both clock a lot higher and both do much more IPC. There might not be a large difference between 10900k and Ryzen, if you only take a 10+ game average.
But if you look at the games individually (as we should, because we don't experience the games "in average"), there will be games with 20%+ differences. Some games perform equally, but in some there are very noticeable difference even at 1440p, and that's compared against faster 3900xt (TechPowerUp).

In my opinion GPU reviews should definitely still be done with the 10900k, as there's a possibility of 20% performance difference (unless you're only testing 4k).

text: Regarding Microsoft Flight Simulator. I wonder how it will run when Valve has all the bugs sorted out in Steam Play in Linux. The thing is, my Ryzen 2500U laptop is severly bottlenecked by CPU/memory bandwidth (I need to downclock the CPU to 1600MHz to get the most out of the GPU due to TDP constraints)... DX9 - DX11 games tend to run really bad, no matter resolution in Windows. Similar to what MFL does with modern computers (Using only four threads properly while at the same time using DX11 that rely heavily on those few threads to prepare draw calls). The thing is, using Steam Play in Linux, games run miraculously  better on my laptop! Valve's translation layer "Proton" translates DirectX to Vulkan, and probably, because of this there's less stress on the CPU making the system more balanced. I wonder if we could witness the same thing with MFL eventually? It would be kind of funny if a Microsoft-developed game runs better on Linux. ;)

text:
I'm not too disappointed by the performance numbers - of course we all assumed that Nvidia showed their best case scenario before launch. However, I am disappointed by the power consumption. It's in line with rumors and expectations, but I still would have hoped for lower consumption.
I'm sure a lot of people will tell me the usual things I hear in any discussion about power consumption - saying that it's a silly thing to worry about, that it won't be noticeable on your power bill, as long as the cooler is good there's no reason to care about the extra heat, et cetera. But I do care... I use my computer in a smallish room without direct access to air conditioning, and I know from experience what a difference an extra 100+ watts of heat makes in the summer. 327 watts in game for a single graphics card is massive and it will kick out a lot of heat and I'm sure it'll be noticeable for anyone using their computer in similar conditions.
I'm hoping that the rumors are true and AMD have managed to make more efficient graphics cards this time around. It wouldn't be the first time they've managed to significantly beat Nvidia on power efficiency, and while it's been a while since the last time it happened I can at least hope that they can better leverage their node advantage this time around, even if they failed at delivering good power efficiency with the first iteration of RDNA. Otherwise I'll just wait another generation to upgrade. I would like higher framerates, but as a quiet aircooling aficionado who can't stand the heat I feel like north of 300 watts is just not for me. The 3070 might be manageable, but either way I'll definitely wait to see what AMD has. There's always hope :)

@akyhne  I AM a content creator on another channel, I'm intimately familiar with the process. The creator does not choose the number and place of the ads.

What they can choose is to enable pre, mid, or post-roll ads, and mark where mid-roll ad breaks would be least disruptive IF SHOWN.

That very different from specifically choosing how many appear.  You could get 1 ad, or you could get 12 - out of the creators' control. It could be different for every viewer, and it could be different every time YOU view the same video, too.

The only way to avoid mid-roll ads entirely is to disable them, entirely - which is not really an option as you are cutting off a major part of YT ad revenue by doing so. Many creators leave the mid-roll ad placement on automatic placement, which is generated by YT.

text:
There are two MAJOR questions everyone is asking:

- How much better it is than the existing 20 series? Steve just gave us that answer. I think it is a good upgrade in regards to 20 series, albeit this is xx80 model, and 80 Ti will surely come.
- How the next GPU from AMD, the BIG Navi will cope with this new 30 series?

Hmm, let's speculate. From what I know, the next big chip will have double the CUs of the 5700 XT. It will run on 2Ghz+ game frequency (if future game consoles are any indication). Should have 50% better power efficiency. And should probably have 5-10% better IP performance.
So that gives us somewhere from 1.6x (less optimistic) to 2.46x (super optimistic, gains from 2xCU + higher freq+better IP)

In the benchmarks that Steve presented, 3080 is on average faster than 5700XT. 
- in 1440p 64% faster. So here we see that even the less optimistic speculation (60% better) is attenable by AMD. AMD could end up being faster than 3080 model.
- in 4K 3080 is  92% faster than 5700XT. In 4K, numbers are less in favor of AMD being to attending the performance of 3080, though not completely out of question.

Now, I know what you will say, bit 3080 has double the number of shaders than 2080Ti and it is only 1.317 times faster! Sure, But I am looking at 2080Ti vs 2060S (they have also that 2x shaders more thing going for them), and there 2080Ti is 1.7 faster than 2060S. AMD is going from medium range to high end, and the difference will be bigger. Nvidia has diminishing results as they already had a quite big CU number with 2080 Ti to start with. AMD is probably bringing better IP performance which Nvidia seems missed here. 

So yes, I would wait for what AMD has to show.

Thanks Steve for another great review.

PS: I said it is my speculation, not hard facts)

text:
Reviews so far are what I expected, the results for me (a 4K PC gamer) 25-32% better than 2080ti is very much underwhelming (based on double the CUDA cores, 2nd generation of RT cores and 3rd generation of tensor cores), but that underwhelming feeling is countered by the amazing price-to-performance vs Turing.
So expect 2 sets of reviews 
(1) these cards are great 32% better than 2080ti for $700 or 
(2) for all the doubling of cores and node shrink it doesn't quite hit the mark when it comes to all the hype.

Fairly expected evolution in these compute/data center GPUs from Volta (16nm) to Turing (12nm really 16nm) to Ampere (8nm). And funny enough AI/ML was exactly why I pre-ordered my RTX 2080ti. When Jensen was on stage talking in 2018, I didn't see a gaming GPU, I saw a cut down Titan V at half the price with a few improvements. And the old hardware database tables (as confirmed by Nvidia technical support) in Ubuntu 18.04 actually recognize the RTX 2080ti as a GV102 chip not TU102.

text:
@Luthi_YC  Based on all the things we know. 
We know RDNA2 is much more efficient then RDNA1 and therefore more efficient then ampere. 
We also know that there are 2 cards with dual 8 pins. 
This means that the higher end is at least 270W or so. 
270W + higeher efficiency = close to 3080
if they make a 300W card its gonna beat the 3080. 

We can also analyze it from another angle. 
We know that 40 CUs of RDNA1 is faster then a 2070. We also know that RDNA2 will have higher clockspeed at about 2.2Ghz and higher IPC. 
That will make a 40CU card at least as fast as a 2080S, maybe a bit faster.
 
Now what happens with double CU count at 80 like we know it will have? 
Well the performance won't double with doubling the CUs but it will indeed improve significantly. 
With 3080 kinda sucking at 1440p AMD can make a faster 1440p card no doubt about it. 
But can they beat 3090? Maybe but the chance is not that high imo.

author: @hi_tech_reptilezz

text: @hi_tech_reptilezz  On TSMC, it would be slightly more costly, per die basis. But you would be getting 65M transistor/mm2 instead of 44M. All those extra transistors would have made a massive performance difference, so in the end, you may end up with a $800 or $900 GPU, that is much faster than the 3080 and Jensen would still have high profit margins.
author: @nerdtechgasm6502

text: @hi_tech_reptilezz  Basically if Jensen could do RTX Ampere with TSMC 7N, gamers would benefit with more perf & more perf/w. It would also make it extremely difficult or impossible for AMD to compete with RDNA 2. Samsung 8N just leaves the door open for AMD.
author: @nerdtechgasm6502

text:
@16xthedetail76  "But it was also a no brainer since TMSC is pretty backed up"
The problem is that Nvidia probably would have been better off paying the premium for TSMC 7nm, because even though each die would be up to about $50 more expensive, Nvidia wouldn't have needed to put a $150 cooler on every card, so would have had a better product at lower overall cost.
